claims.text: High configurational entropy ensures a uniform, single-phase crystal structure in high-entropy alloys.
A uniform, single-phase crystal structure enhances electron–phonon coupling.
High configurational entropy promotes robust type-II superconductivity at low temperature.
Reducing configurational entropy by selective elemental substitution will lower or suppress the superconducting transition.
The starting alloy is near-equiatomic and has high mixing entropy.
The starting alloy is an as-cast, homogeneous, disordered, single-phase alloy.
Partial elemental substitution can reduce configurational entropy while preserving the overall crystal structure and a similar average valence-electron count.
The relevant superconducting transition should occur at or below approximately 10 K under ambient pressure.
High configurational entropy maintains a chemically homogeneous, single-phase crystalline state.
High configurational entropy minimizes local chemical fluctuations.
Minimizing local chemical fluctuations reduces electron scattering.
Reduced electron scattering enhances electron–phonon coupling and favors Cooper pairing.
Reducing configurational entropy compromises the uniform electronic environment and makes superconductivity less robust.
The high-entropy variant will exhibit a superconducting transition marked by a sharp resistance drop and strong diamagnetic response.
The high-entropy variant will have a higher critical temperature and more robust superconductivity than the reduced-entropy control.
The proposed mechanism is limited to near-equiatomic, single-phase alloys that retain structural homogeneity and may fail following phase separation or substantial structural inhomogeneity.
The magnitude of changes in critical temperature and other superconducting parameters may depend on composition and processing.
Failure of the high-entropy sample to show a higher or more robust transition than the reduced-entropy control would falsify the proposed entropy-enhancement hypothesis.
